subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 55-year-old man undergoes colectomy for adenocarcinoma of the descending colon. Tumor sequencing identifies a C to T transition at a CpG dinucleotide within a tumor suppressor gene, and the remainder of the gene sequence is intact; the change creates a premature stop codon. He has no family history of colorectal cancer and no known exposure to carcinogens.
question: Which of the following chemical events most likely produced this base change?

options.text: Depurination of guanine with loss of the purine ring
Ultraviolet light-induced formation of a thymine dimer
Deamination of cytosine to uracil, generating a U:G mismatch
Methylation of cytosine within the promoter region

explanation_correct: Spontaneous hydrolytic deamination of cytosine converts it to uracil and creates a U:G mismatch; if the uracil is not excised before replication, adenine is inserted opposite it, fixing a C to T transition. Deamination of 5-methylcytosine, which is common at CpG dinucleotides, directly yields thymine and is the single most frequent source of C to T transitions in human tumors.

explanation_incorrect.A: Depurination removes a base and leaves an abasic site that typically produces transversions or strand breaks rather than an isolated transition at a CpG dinucleotide.
explanation_incorrect.B: Thymine dimers follow ultraviolet exposure and yield tandem CC to TT mutations typical of skin cancers, not a single C to T transition in a colon tumor.
explanation_incorrect.D: Oxidation of guanine gives 8-oxoguanine, which mispairs with adenine and produces G to C or G to T transversions.
explanation_incorrect.E: Methylation of cytosine to 5-methylcytosine is a normal epigenetic modification that does not alter base-pairing specificity, although it predisposes the base to deamination-induced transitions.

educationalObjective: Deamination of cytosine or 5-methylcytosine produces C to T transitions, the most common single-base substitution in human tumors.
